Licence, transparency, and the hazard that travels with a protocol

Screens 24–26. One of these carries an open question the design deliberately does not answer for you: the CC0-versus-CC BY default for external contributions is still undecided in the legal framework, so both options are presented with equal weight and neither is pre-selected.

24 LICENCE FOR AN EXTERNAL CONTRIBUTION (N22) 1440 × 700 · OPEN DECISION · neither option is pre-selected
UNRESOLVED IN THE LEGAL FRAMEWORK The default licence for contributions to someone else's artifact is not yet decided by SciCollab. This screen presents both candidates neutrally so the founders and counsel can choose. Nothing below should be read as a recommendation.
the moment of contribution · P. Aguirre is adding a failure mode to MC-0288, a card they do not own
CC0 1.0
public domain dedication · no conditions
You waive all rights in your contribution. Anyone may use it for anything, without attributing you.
ARGUMENTS FOR
No attribution stacking. A card with 40 contributors under CC BY accumulates 40 attribution obligations, and downstream users cannot comply in practice.
Legally simplest for reuse in commercial and clinical settings, where licence review is a real cost.
Matches what most data repositories now recommend for metadata and small factual contributions.
ARGUMENTS AGAINST
Contributors get no enforceable right to be named — and this platform's entire thesis is that credit for small contributions should be real.
Not accepted by some institutions' IP policies, which may prevent staff contributing at all.
Irreversible. A waiver cannot be withdrawn.
In practice attribution would still be displayed by the platform — but as a convention we could change, not a right the contributor holds.
CC BY 4.0
attribution required · everything else permitted
You keep copyright. Anyone may use your contribution for any purpose provided they credit you.
ARGUMENTS FOR
Credit becomes a right rather than a courtesy, which is consistent with everything else the product does about attribution.
Familiar to researchers, accepted by essentially every institutional IP policy and funder mandate.
The contributor keeps standing to object if their work is misused.
ARGUMENTS AGAINST
Attribution stacking is a genuine problem at scale, and a widely forked card could become impractical to reuse compliantly.
Licence compatibility questions when a card mixes CC BY contributions with CC0 or proprietary material.
Creates a real, if small, legal risk for downstream commercial users — which may suppress exactly the reuse we want.
A middle path exists — CC BY with a platform-level collective attribution notice — but it is untested and would need counsel's view.
WHAT THE CONTRIBUTOR SEES TODAY
You are adding a failure mode to a card owned by T. Okafor. Choose how your contribution is licensed:
CC0 1.0
CC BY 4.0
Neither is pre-selected. The contribution cannot be submitted until one is chosen, and the choice is remembered as a preference — never applied silently the first time.
Shown at the moment of contribution, not buried in account settings, because this is the only moment the person is thinking about this specific piece of work.
WHAT WE NEED FROM YOU
A decision on the default — the pre-selected option for a user who has expressed no preference. The interface above works either way; only the initial state changes.
Also needed: whether an institution can force one choice for its staff. Some IP policies will require it, and the policy defaults table has a row waiting for it.
RELATED, ALSO OPEN
N23 database right. The EU sui generis database right may attach to the corpus as a whole. Who holds it — the platform, the institution, or nobody — is a separate unresolved question with its own clause in the terms.

THE NUMBERS THAT MATTER MOST ARE THE UNFLATTERING ONES
14 of 41 appeals were upheld — we got it wrong a third of the time we were challenged. A transparency report with a 2% overturn rate means the appeal process is not working, and publishing 34% is the point of publishing at all.
Two government requests, neither complied with. Both were for user identity, both refused for want of a valid legal basis, and both are reported here as the DSA and our own policy require. A warrant canary is maintained alongside.

26 HAZARD DATA (N16) AND LIABILITY (N17) 660 × 620 · attached to the protocol, travels with every fork
HAZARD AND LIABILITY MC-0288 v7 · before you run it
GHS HAZARDS · 3 MATERIALS
Lipofectamine 3000
H315 skin irritation · H319 serious eye irritation · SDS
HEK293T · BSL-1
human-derived cell line · handle as potentially infectious
Genetically modified material
contained-use notification may be required in your jurisdiction
Hazard data forks with the card. Every derivative of MC-0288 inherits these three, and a fork cannot remove them — only add. That is the whole reason to attach hazards to the protocol rather than to a separate safety document nobody opens.
LIABILITY · N17 · SHOWN ONCE PER CARD
This protocol was contributed by a researcher, not by SciCollab. It has not been verified or approved by us, and it is not a substitute for your own risk assessment or your institution's safety approval.
I have read the hazards and will follow my institution's procedures
WHY NOT A BANNER
A liability notice on every page is wallpaper. Once per card, at first use, with a checkbox that is recorded — that is a notice someone actually reads.
LINKED, NOT DUPLICATED
Hazards come from the inventory record for each material. One source, so a corrected SDS updates every protocol using it.
